analysis.one_liner: Cuts individual and corporate tax rates, repeals the estate tax and a tax on investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved after introduction: zero cosponsors, no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the tax code to sharply cut rates across the board: three individual brackets of 12%, 25%, and 29% (replacing seven brackets topping out at 39.6%), a corporate rate cut from 35% to 15%, and a 15% cap on tax for income earned through partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships. It repeals the estate tax and the 3.8% net investment income tax, lets businesses deduct equipment costs immediately, and shifts U.S. taxation of multinational corporations to a system that largely exempts foreign profits. It contains no provision to raise revenue to replace any of the cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, whose tax rate would fall from 35% to 15% and whose foreign subsidiary profits would be almost entirely exempt from U.S. tax; owners of large estates and very wealthy households, who would no longer pay the estate tax or the 3.8% tax on investment income; and owners of pass-through businesses, whose business income would be taxed at no more than 15%. Middle- and lower-income filers would also see their rates reduced under the new 12%/25%/29% brackets, though the largest dollar savings would flow to the highest earners and to owners of capital.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, large estates, and high earners

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 15% and caps the tax on business income earned through partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships at 15% [S3]
Replaces the seven-bracket individual rate structure (10% through 39.6%) with three brackets of 12%, 25%, and 29%, lowering rates at every income level [S3]
Repeals the estate tax for people dying after 2016 while keeping the step-up in basis, so heirs would owe no tax on either the estate or its unrealized gains [S3]
Repeals the 3.8% net investment income tax, a surtax paid by households with high investment income [S3]
Lets businesses deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment immediately rather than over years, and elect any shorter depreciation period [S3]

Moves the taxation of multinational profits to a participation-exemption system: dividends from foreign subsidiaries would be 95% deductible, and accumulated offshore earnings would be taxed once at a reduced rate, payable over eight years [S3]
Makes a change in a corporation's legal form a tax-free event as long as the owners and assets stay the same [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Future taxpayers and the federal government. The bill raises no revenue anywhere in its text — every provision cuts or eliminates a tax — so the lost money would have to be made up by borrowing, by future tax increases, or by cuts to government programs. The largest individual savings would go to the households with the highest incomes, so the burden of making up the difference would fall disproportionately on everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offset of any kind; every title reduces or repeals a tax, so the entire cost would land on deficits or future offsets [S3]

Its largest provisions are concentrated at the top: the estate tax applied only to the largest estates, the 3.8% investment income tax applied only to high-income households, and the corporate and foreign-profits cuts flow to owners of corporate stock [S3]
Flattening the individual brackets to 12%/25%/29% cuts the top rate from 39.6% to 29% while raising the bottom rate from 10% to 12%, so the rate relief is weighted toward the highest earners [S3]
Repealing the net investment income tax removes revenue collected from high-income households' capital gains, dividends, and other investment earnings [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ordinary filers would see real, if modest, rate cuts under the new individual brackets, and businesses of all sizes would benefit from immediate expensing. But the bill's biggest money moves — a 35%-to-15% corporate rate cut, near-total exemption of foreign profits, estate tax repeal, and repeal of the investment income tax — go almost entirely to corporations and the wealthiest households, and the bill offers no mechanism to pay for any of it. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that this is a very large unfinanced tax cut whose savings skew heavily toward concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the tax-writing committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on November 14, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5]
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's life [S4]

The committee took no further action — there is no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote in the bill's complete action history — and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained through this bill itself, since it never advanced. Its main beneficiaries would have been corporations, large estates, and high-income investors; broadly similar corporate and individual rate cuts were enacted weeks after its introduction through separate legislation, without this bill's estate tax or investment income repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply never moved

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no cosponsors ever joined, so only the Republican sponsor's support is on the record; no member or bloc is recorded as opposing it.

industries.note: A 15% corporate rate plus a 95% deduction on dividends from foreign subsidiaries and a reduced-rate settlement of stockpiled offshore earnings would have sharply cut the tax owed on profits booked abroad. That revenue gap would be borne by other taxpayers or by borrowing.

Repeal of the estate tax, paired with retention of basis step-up, means inherited wealth would never face tax at either transfer or sale. Repeal of the 3.8% net investment income tax similarly benefits only households with substantial investment income.

Partnership, S corporation, and sole proprietorship income would be taxed at no more than 15%, far below the top individual rate this bill would replace. The benefit scales with how much business income an owner has.
Immediate expensing and shorter depreciation elections let companies deduct equipment costs upfront, encouraging investment. The cost arrives indirectly as lost federal revenue.
